sections.text: You played a classical line with 3.Bc4 and 4.Bb3, which met 3...Be6 by trading bishops. After 5.axb3 the open a-file gave you something to aim at, and you were comfortably around +0.3.
You kept developing smoothly with 6.d4, 8.Qxd4, 9.Bg5 and 11.Qd3, a sensible plan. 10.O-O?! was a small inaccuracy, because 10.Rxa7 was available, but your position remained fine.
Black went wrong with 15...Nd7?, and you reacted immediately with 16.Qxd5!. That queen move pinned the knight on d7 to the queen on d8 and won a pawn, taking the evaluation to nearly +2.

17.Qxb7?! was a little greedy, since 17.Qf3 was cleaner, but your opponent then blundered with 17...Bg5??. You answered 18.Bxg5! hxg5, a trade that left you well ahead. From there you doubled with 19.Rad1, built pressure and won with 22.Nxc5.

review.turning_point: 16.Qxd5! punished 15...Nd7 by taking a pawn with tempo, and 18.Bxg5! after 17...Bg5?? kept you clearly ahead.
review.focus: On move 17, 17.Qxb7 grabbed a second pawn but left the queen far from the king. Compare it with 17.Qf3, which kept more control.

review.headline: A Philidor where you took over after a sharp tactic, then lost on time while winning

sections.text: You played a flexible setup with a bishop on g4 and a fianchetto. By 9...Be6?! and 10...d5?! you were already slightly loose, and 11...dxe4?? let White play 12.gxf6, swinging the evaluation to -3.6. The better answer was 11...d4.

Even so, you fought. White's 15.Bxe5?? was a serious mistake, and you found 15...Nxe5!, a discovered attack because moving the d7 knight uncovered your queen on the d8 square against the knight on d6. That swung things back in your favor.
You went on to win material with 18.O-O-O Qxb7. The position stayed good for you, but 23...Bf8? was a slip and 24...Kc8?? left a piece to be won; 24...Kc7 was safer.

Later White blundered with 27.Qe7??, and 27...Bxe7 was the move to play. Instead 27...Rd8?? let White back in. By the end you were in time trouble and lost on the clock after 31.Kd2, in a game that you were winning by a lot.

review.turning_point: 15...Nxe5! turned the game around after 11...dxe4?? had put you in trouble, and 27...Rd8?? threw away a clearly winning chance.
review.focus: When the clock gets low, look for the one forcing move. On move 27, 27...Bxe7 simply took the queen, but it was missed under time pressure.

review.headline: A fast Italian win: your opponent grabbed pawns and then hung the queen

sections.text: You played the Italian with 3.Bc4 and your opponent replied with 3...d5, a sharp central break. You took it with 4.exd5, and the evaluation moved to +1.4 for you.
Black then played 4...Nb4, attacking c2, but you calmly developed with 5.Nc3. That solid move kept everything covered, and it was the right way to respond to a loose-looking attack.
Your opponent went on with 5...Nxd5?, which let you play 6.Nxd5 and win a knight for a pawn. The better try was 5...c6, but after the exchange you were up around three points of material.
Black then lost the thread completely with 6...Qg5? and you finished with 7.Nxg5!, taking the queen. You answered both opponent errors accurately and the game ended almost at once.

review.turning_point: 6.Nxd5 won a piece, and 7.Nxg5! after 6...Qg5? won the queen and finished the game.
review.focus: You played this cleanly. A good habit to keep is the one you showed at move 5, calmly developing with 5.Nc3 instead of reacting to the knight on b4.

sections.text: Your opponent chose the Stafford Gambit and played 3...Nc6?, which you answered perfectly. After 4.Nxc6! dxc6 5.d3 you were already around +1.8 and had a healthy extra pawn.
6.Be3? was the first slip, and the stronger move was 6.Be2. After that, 6...Bb6 gave you a second chance, and you built up with 7.Nc3, 8.Be2 and 9.Qd2, still holding about +2.5.

The decisive blunder was 10.h3??. It lost the advantage because the better move, 10.Bxg4, simply took the knight. After 10...Nxe3 11.fxe3! you recovered well, and when 13...Bxh3 came you played the clean 14.gxh3, which kept you clearly better.

With a big lead you went wrong again at move 18. 18.Ne2?? moved the knight off c3 and uncovered the bishop on a5 against your queen on d2, so 18...Bxd2 won your queen and decided the game. 18.Qf2 would have kept you in control.

review.turning_point: 10.h3?? let the knight on g4 off the hook and 18.Ne2?? later opened the bishop on a5 onto your queen, which finished the game.
review.focus: Before moving a knight that is guarding something, look at what it blocks. On move 18 the knight on c3 stood between a bishop and your queen.

review.headline: An even Vienna where you won a piece and attacked, then dropped the queen and ran short of time

sections.text: You answered the Vienna with a classical setup, and after 3.Bc4 you traded your light-squared bishop for White's with 3...Be6 and 4...Bxc4. That kept things calm and left you equal, around -0.5 for Black.

The first big moment came at 6.Nd5??, where White put the knight on d5 and walked into trouble. Taking with 6...Nxd5 was natural but not best; 6...Nxe4 was stronger. The recapture 7.cxd5 let White off the hook and the evaluation drifted back near equal.

You still played active chess, and 11...Nxe4 followed by 13...Qxb2 grabbed pawns and put you ahead on material. By then you were around +2 and had real winning chances, although your queen was far from home.

Then came 14...Qa3??. The queen walked into 15.Qb5+ and the position collapsed to -5.8. Instead, 14...Nc3 would have forked the queen on e2 and rook on b1 and kept you in the game. You then lost on time in a position that was already difficult.

review.turning_point: 14...Qa3?? took the queen out of play and let 15.Qb5+ in, while 14...Nc3 forking the queen and rook was the way to keep your edge.
review.focus: On move 14, before moving the queen again, look at what a knight jump like 14...Nc3 attacks. Candidate moves that hit two pieces at once deserve a look before a queen raid.

review.headline: A Philidor where you got a big edge, converted it into a huge material lead, and then lost to a mate in the final moves

sections.text: You met the Philidor with a classical setup: bishop to c4, d4 and the queen to e2. Your opponent answered with 3...h6 and 6...c5, and then went wrong at once with 7...Bd7??, which jumped the evaluation to +3.4 in your favor.

You did not get the most out of that gift. 8.Bf4 was fine looking but gave back a lot; the sharper 8.e5 was the way to punish the bishop on d7. Even so, you stayed clearly better and kept the pressure with 9.Bxb5 and 10.Qxb5+.

The decisive moment came when your opponent played 16...Qe7??. You spotted the shot immediately with 17.Bxc7!, and after 18.Qxe7+ you were far ahead in material. That was real tactical alertness, and the rest of the middlegame was a matter of keeping control.

You pushed on, picked up the a-pawn with 31.Rxa7 and stood close to +5. Then 33.Ree7?? doubled rooks on the seventh but allowed 33...Rd1+, a forced mate. A quiet move like 33.Ra3 would have kept everything under control.

review.turning_point: 17.Bxc7! after 16...Qe7?? turned a small edge into a crushing material lead, and 33.Ree7?? then threw it all away by walking into a forced mate.
review.focus: Before every move in a winning position, check the opponent's checks and forcing replies. On move 33 a single look at 33...Rd1+ would have shown the mate and kept you at +4.8.

10.Ne6 was a blunder, since 10...Bxe6 simply won a piece. 10...Qh4 missed it, and 11.Nxf8 followed. You found 11...Bxf2+ and 12.Kf1 12...Bxe1, then 13...Qxe1+ 14.Kxe1 14...Kxf8, leaving you well ahead.

review.focus: 51...Rxf2 took a bishop and ignored the a7 pawn. In a won endgame, count the opponent's passed pawns first; 51...Bc8 kept it safe. Also watch the clock.

review.headline: Opposite-side castling turns into a rapid queenside breakthrough

sections.text: After a quiet Vienna opening, the game ignited when your opponent chose opposite-side castling with 9.O-O-O. You immediately launched your queenside pawns forward with 9...a5. Both sides overlooked tactical chances around the e6-pawn, but the race toward the kings quickly took over the board.

Your advance with 11...a3 cracked open White's shelter on the b-file. After White pushed 13.g5, your retreat 13...Ne8 unleashed a discovered attack down the f-file against the knight on f3. White tried to reposition with 15.Na4, but this left the knight directly in the path of 15...b5.

White ignored the threat on the flank and pushed 16.h5, allowing you to win a piece with 16...bxa4. You then activated your bishop with 18...Bb4 and 19...Bc3 to control key squares near White's king. After 21...Qb4 created decisive threats on the open b-file, White resigned.

review.turning_point: White's blunder 16.h5 allowed you to play 16...bxa4, winning a piece and breaking through the defense around the white king.
review.focus: Keep an eye on tactical vulnerabilities in your camp during the opening, such as the loose e6-pawn after 8...Nbd7.

sections.text: You handled the Caro-Kann Exchange Variation smoothly. After 3.exd5 cxd5, you developed your pieces naturally and gained the bishop pair with 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Bxf3, keeping the position completely balanced.

review.turning_point: There was no decisive chess mistake on the board; the game was decided entirely when your clock expired after 13...Qc7.
review.focus: In bullet time controls, trust your opening instincts faster so you don't fall behind on the clock in balanced setups like the one reached after 10.Re1.

sections.text: You played the Italian with 3.Bc4, and Black answered with the early 3...Qf6. After 4.Nc3 4...Nge7 5.d4 5...exd4 you were fine.
6.Bg5 hit the knight with the queen behind it, but 6.Nb5 was stronger. After 6...Qd6 7.Nb5 7...Qb4+ came 8.c3, a blunder that left a piece to be won; 8.Nd2 was the move. 8...Qxc4 took the bishop.
You fought back with 9.Nxc7+ 9...Kd8 10.Nxa8. Black's 11...f6 was a mistake, because 11...Qxe4+ was stronger, and your 12.Rxc3! skewered the queen on c4 and the knight on c6.
14.Nd2 was the final blunder, leaving a piece to be won; 14.Rc3 was the way. After 14...fxg5 15.Qh5 15...Qxb2 you were lost.

review.turning_point: 8.c3 allowed 8...Qxc4, and the lost bishop left you a piece down.
review.focus: 8.c3 blocked a defender and left the c4 bishop loose. When a queen checks on b4, look at which pieces it can take next, and 8.Nd2 kept the position safe.

review.headline: A French Exchange where you hunted Black's king and finished with mate

sections.text: You played the French Exchange with 3.exd5, 4.Nf3 and 5.Bb5, and after 5...Bd7 6.Nc3 6...Nf6 7.Bg5 you built a solid position. 8.O-O and 9.Re1 were slightly slow, but 10.Bxc6 and 11.Ne5 kept the initiative.

13.Bxe7 was a good capture, and Black replied 13...Qxe7, a blunder (+0.4 to +5.7); 13...Nxc3 was the right move. You then played 14.Nxe4, a blunder that gave up much of the lead (+5.7 to +1.8); 14.Nxd5 was the best.
Even so, 15.Qxe4 15...Bb5 16.Qxb7! kept the initiative. 17.Qxc7 17...Rfe8 was another Black error, and you found 18.Qxf7+!, a strong shot that opened the king.
Then you handled a long attack. 23.Qh3 kept pressure on h7, and 24...Qc3 was an error and you found 25.Qxc3!. 27.Nf7+, 28.Rf5 and 30.Nh6+ carried the attack, and 43.Qf7# ended the game with mate.

review.turning_point: 13...Qxe7 was a blunder, and your 16.Qxb7! and 18.Qxf7+! kept the attack going.
review.focus: 14.Nxe4 swapped off a strong knight when 14.Nxd5 kept the advantage. In a won position, look for the strongest capture instead of the first natural trade.
